questions.title: Sample Exam · S1
questions.promptMarkdown: Which of the following best reflects the Big Five trait of agreeableness?
options: A high level of competitiveness and assertiveness in team discussions
A preference for cooperative, trusting, and prosocial interactions
A tendency to work best in solitary, analytical tasks
A propensity to challenge leadership and resist feedback
A high need for control and emotional impulsivity
hints: Think about the interpersonal warmth dimension of the Big Five (`OCEAN`), contrasting high-agreeableness cooperation with competitive or antagonistic behaviors.
Check whose behavior is being explained (only another person = FAE; comparing self vs. other = actor–observer; one trait coloring all ratings = halo).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: B** — *A preference for cooperative, trusting, and prosocial interactions.*
- **Why B works:** Agreeableness captures cooperativeness, warmth, trust, and good-natured prosocial orientation toward others (`R&J Ch. 5`).
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` reflects low agreeableness / high dominance or competitiveness rather than agreeableness.
  - `C` describes introversion (lower Extraversion) plus analytical focus, not agreeableness.
  - `D` describes low agreeableness (antagonism/disagreeableness) or low openness to feedback.
  - `E` combines high need for dominance with low Emotional Stability (high Neuroticism / impulsivity).
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: reflects low agreeableness / high dominance or competitiveness rather than agreeableness.

questions.title: Sample Exam · S2
questions.promptMarkdown: Which organizational structure combines functional specialization with project-based teams?
options: Network structure
Boundaryless organization
Matrix structure
Modular organization
Flat structure
hints: Recall which structure intentionally breaks *unity of command* so employees report to both a functional department head and a product/project manager.
Match standardized, cost-focused work to formal/centralized mechanics, and uncertain, innovative work to decentralized cross-functional designs.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: C** — *Matrix structure.*
- **Why C works:** A **matrix structure** overlays product/project departmentalization onto functional departmentalization, creating dual lines of authority (violating unity of command) to coordinate specialists across projects.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` (*Network* / *Virtual*) outsources major business functions to external partners around a small core organization.
  - `B` (*Boundaryless*) seeks to eliminate internal vertical/horizontal chains and external boundaries altogether.
  - `D` (*Modular*) resembles virtual/outsourced component assembly rather than dual internal functional-plus-project reporting.
  - `E` (*Flat*) refers simply to few hierarchical levels (wide span of control), not dual functional/project teams.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: (*Network* / *Virtual*) outsources major business functions to external partners around a small core organization.

questions.title: Sample Exam · S3
questions.promptMarkdown: Under expectancy theory, employee motivation is highest when:
options: Rewards are externally imposed regardless of performance
Employees believe effort will improve performance and lead to valued outcomes
Managers issue frequent directives
Goals are assigned without employee involvement
Performance evaluations are standardized across teams
hints: Vroom's Expectancy Theory multiplies three beliefs: $\text{Motivation} = \text{Expectancy} \times \text{Instrumentality} \times \text{Valence}$. What must all three links be?
Check whether the driver comes from task enjoyment itself, fairness of rules/voice vs. outcomes, or multiplying effort-to-performance-to-reward beliefs.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: B** — *Employees believe effort will improve performance and lead to valued outcomes.*
- **Why B works:** "Effort will improve performance" is **Expectancy** ($E \to P$), "lead to outcomes" is **Instrumentality** ($P \to O$), and "valued" is **Valence** ($V$). Motivation peaks when all three are strongly positive.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` destroys **Instrumentality** ($P \to O = 0$): if rewards arrive regardless of performance, effort does not pay off.
  - `C` describes directive leadership style, not expectancy-instrumentality-valence links.
  - `D` relates to Goal-Setting Theory / participation, not Vroom's three cognitive links.
  - `E` reflects procedural standardization in appraisal, not the three expectancy multipliers.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: destroys **Instrumentality** ($P \to O = 0$): if rewards arrive regardless of performance, effort does not pay off.

questions.title: Sample Exam · S4
questions.promptMarkdown: A team member holds power because they possess specialized knowledge and skills that others rely on. This is an example of:
options: Legitimate power
Coercive power
Expert power
Referent power
Reward power
hints: French & Raven divide power into formal (`Coercive`, `Reward`, `Legitimate`) and personal (`Expert`, `Referent`). Notice the dependency is built on *knowledge and skills*.
Separate formal position power (legitimate/reward/coercive) from personal power (expert/referent), and weigh resource nonsubstitutability plus each side's walk-away alternative.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: C** — *Expert power.*
- **Why C works:** **Expert power** is personal power derived from unique expertise, special skills, or knowledge that others depend on.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` (*Legitimate*) rests on formal hierarchical position/title.
  - `B` (*Coercive*) rests on fear of negative outcomes or punishment.
  - `D` (*Referent*) rests on admiration, charisma, and interpersonal identification.
  - `E` (*Reward*) rests on control over valued positive distributions (pay, promotions, praise).
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: (*Legitimate*) rests on formal hierarchical position/title.

questions.title: Sample Exam · S5
questions.promptMarkdown: A leader avoids making decisions, offers little direction, and frequently delays responses to team issues. This reflects:
options: Autocratic leadership
Transformational leadership
Laissez-faire leadership
Transactional leadership
Servant leadership
hints: In Bass & Avolio's Full Range of Leadership Model, which style represents the *abdication of responsibility* and active non-involvement?
Verify whether the theory treats leader style as fixed (requiring situational engineering) or adaptable to follower readiness and task ambiguity.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: C** — *Laissez-faire leadership.*
- **Why C works:** **Laissez-faire** is the absence of leadership: abdicating responsibilities, avoiding decisions, and providing minimal guidance.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` (*Autocratic*) makes unilateral decisions and gives strict direction.
  - `B` (*Transformational*) actively inspires, stimulates intellectually, and coaches individually.
  - `D` (*Transactional*) actively clarifies roles, rewards goal achievement (*contingent reward*), or monitors deviations (*management by exception*).
  - `E` (*Servant*) actively prioritizes follower growth and service, not avoidance.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: (*Autocratic*) makes unilateral decisions and gives strict direction.

questions.title: Sample Exam · S6
questions.promptMarkdown: A manager consistently treats employees fairly, communicates respectfully, and explains the reasoning behind organizational decisions transparently. Which concept does this best illustrate?
options: Procedural justice
Interactional justice
Retributive justice
Corrective justice
Equity theory
hints: Separate structural process rules from *how* a manager treats and informs people face-to-face (`interpersonal` dignity + `informational` transparent explanations).
Check whether the driver comes from task enjoyment itself, fairness of rules/voice vs. outcomes, or multiplying effort-to-performance-to-reward beliefs.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: B** — *Interactional justice.*
- **Why B works:** **Interactional justice** is the degree to which employees are treated with dignity and respect (**interpersonal justice**) and given truthful, transparent explanations for decisions (**informational justice**). Notice both cues appear in the stem ("communicates respectfully" + "explains the reasoning ... transparently").
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` (*Procedural justice*) focuses on the fairness of the formal *process/rules* used to determine outcomes (e.g., voice, consistency, bias suppression), whereas respect + candid explanations specifically define *interactional* justice.
  - `C` and `D` refer to legal/punishment doctrines outside the R&J three-part organizational justice framework.
  - `E` (*Equity theory*) evaluates perceived outcome-to-input ratios relative to a referent other, not respectful explanation quality.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: (*Procedural justice*) focuses on the fairness of the formal *process/rules* used to determine outcomes (e.g., voice, consistency, bias suppression), whereas respect + candid explanations specifically define *interactional* justice.

questions.title: Sample Exam · S7
questions.promptMarkdown: A software development team continues to invest time and money into a failing technical solution primarily because of the resources they have already committed. Which decision-making bias is most evident?
options: Overconfidence bias
Anchoring bias
Escalation of commitment
Bounded rationality
Representativeness heuristic
hints: When negative feedback arrives but decision-makers keep throwing good resources after bad because of sunk investments or reluctance to admit a prior choice failed, what is it called?
Ask whether the decision-maker stops at the first 'good enough' threshold under time pressure, filters out disconfirming data, or throws good money after sunk costs.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: C** — *Escalation of commitment.*
- **Why C works:** **Escalation of commitment** is sticking with a failing course of action due to prior sunk investments and psychological reluctance to admit error.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` (*Overconfidence*) is overestimating one's accuracy or success odds initially, not specifically continuing because of sunk resources.
  - `B` (*Anchoring*) is over-relying on an initial number/piece of information when adjusting estimates.
  - `D` (*Bounded rationality*) describes satisficing under time/cognitive limits rather than sinking extra capital into a known failure.
  - `E` (*Representativeness*) judges likelihood by similarity to a stereotype/prototype.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: (*Overconfidence*) is overestimating one's accuracy or success odds initially, not specifically continuing because of sunk resources.

questions.title: Sample Exam · S8
questions.promptMarkdown: Which of the following best describes the primary function of organizational culture?
options: Eliminating all workplace conflict
Reducing employee autonomy
Providing norms that guide member behavior
Increasing dependence on formal rules
Enforcing standardized job descriptions
hints: Culture acts as an internal social control mechanism ("social glue") that coordinates behavior through shared norms even without explicit rulebooks.
Ask whether the prompt describes observable artifacts vs. shared core values, or internal stability vs. external flexibility.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: C** — *Providing norms that guide member behavior.*
- **Why C works:** Organizational culture creates shared meaning, boundary-defining identity, and behavioral norms/sense-making that shape employee attitudes and actions.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` is false: conflict (especially task conflict) persists in healthy organizations.
  - `B` is false: strong cultures actually enable higher autonomy because shared norms replace micromanagement.
  - `D` and `E` confuse *culture* with *formalization* / *bureaucracy*—culture substitutes for explicit written rules rather than increasing dependence on them.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: is false: conflict (especially task conflict) persists in healthy organizations.

questions.title: Sample Exam · S9
questions.promptMarkdown: In group settings, individuals tend to shift their judgments toward more extreme positions after group discussion. This phenomenon is called:
options: Group polarization
Groupthink
Social identification
Deindividuation
Social inhibition
hints: Distinguish *suppressing dissent to keep false harmony* from *discussion amplifying the group's pre-existing leanings toward either more risk or more caution*.
Separate reduced effort in large groups (diffusion of responsibility) from suppressed dissent under unanimity pressure or genuine mutual-accountability synergy.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: A** — *Group polarization.*
- **Why A works:** **Group polarization** (formerly *groupshift*) occurs when discussion amplifies members' initial dominant inclination toward a more extreme conservative or risky position.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `B` (*Groupthink*) is striving for unanimity at the expense of critical appraisal of alternatives, not specifically shifting toward *more extreme* poles after discussion.
  - `C` (*Social identification*) is defining oneself via group membership.
  - `D` (*Deindividuation*) is loss of individual self-awareness in large anonymous crowds.
  - `E` (*Social inhibition*) is worse performance on complex/unfamiliar tasks when others watch.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: (*Groupthink*) is striving for unanimity at the expense of critical appraisal of alternatives, not specifically shifting toward *more extreme* poles after discussion.

questions.title: Sample Exam · S10
questions.promptMarkdown: A manufacturing team operates using standardized procedures and predictable tasks. Under Perrow's model of technology, this reflects:
options: Nonroutine technology
Engineering technology
Routine technology
Craft technology
Adaptive technology
hints: Perrow's `2 × 2` technology model crosses *Task Variability* (few vs. many exceptions) with *Problem Analyzability* (well-defined analytical search vs. unanalyzable intuition). Which cell combines **low exceptions** + **high analyzability**?
Match standardized, cost-focused work to formal/centralized mechanics, and uncertain, innovative work to decentralized cross-functional designs.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: C** — *Routine technology.*
- **Why C works:** Under Perrow's framework (and `R&J Ch. 15` routineness of technology), **routine technology** combines low task variety/predictable steps with high analyzability/standardized procedures.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` (*Nonroutine*) = many exceptions + low analyzability (e.g., exploratory R&D).
  - `B` (*Engineering*) = many exceptions + high analyzability via technical formulas/manuals (e.g., civil bridge design).
  - `D` (*Craft*) = few exceptions + low analyzability requiring tacit intuition (e.g., bespoke woodworking/art).
  - `E` (*Adaptive*) is not one of Perrow's four technology quadrants.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: (*Nonroutine*) = many exceptions + low analyzability (e.g., exploratory R&D).

questions.promptMarkdown: Which leadership theory emphasizes inspiring followers through a shared purpose, intellectual stimulation, and attention to individual needs?
options: Transactional leadership
Transformational leadership
Autocratic leadership
Path-goal theory
Laissez-faire leadership

**Correct Answer: B** — *Transformational leadership.*

  - `C` (*Autocratic*) centralizes decision-making without developmental coaching.
  - `D` (*Path-goal*) adapts directive/supportive/participative/achievement-oriented behaviors to clear obstacles along employee paths, rather than centering the Four I's.
  - `E` (*Laissez-faire*) abdicates leadership altogether.

questions.title: Sample Exam · S12
questions.promptMarkdown: Dr. Ahmed notices that nurse Elena frequently submits patient charts late. Without checking the scheduling logs or speaking with her, he assumes she is simply disorganized and lacks discipline. Later, he learns that Elena has been covering double shifts while caring for a sick family member. Which attribution bias best explains Dr. Ahmed's initial judgment?
options: Self-serving bias
Fundamental attribution error
Confirmation bias
Actor–observer bias
hints: When judging *another person's* behavior, we routinely over-attribute it to internal personality traits ("disorganized") and ignore external situational causes ("double shifts + family illness").
Check whose behavior is being explained (only another person = FAE; comparing self vs. other = actor–observer; one trait coloring all ratings = halo).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: b** — *Fundamental attribution error.*
- **Why b works:** **Fundamental attribution error (FAE)** is underestimating external situational factors while overestimating internal dispositional traits when explaining *someone else's* behavior.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `a` (*Self-serving bias*) is crediting *our own* successes to internal ability and blaming *our own* failures on external luck.
  - `c` (*Confirmation bias*) is seeking evidence that confirms an already-held belief while ignoring disconfirming facts.
  - `d` (*Actor–observer bias*) emphasizes the *asymmetry* between how we explain our own actions (situation) versus another's (traits); here only Dr. Ahmed's observer judgment of Elena is examined, which is the classic textbook definition of FAE.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: (*Self-serving bias*) is crediting *our own* successes to internal ability and blaming *our own* failures on external luck.

questions.title: Sample Exam · S13
questions.promptMarkdown: Laura is the team lead for a product development unit. Initially, she made decisions alone and instructed her team on what to do. Over time, she transitioned to participatory planning, encouraged open dialogue, and integrated team ideas into final deliverables. As a result, team morale and productivity increased. According to OB research on leadership styles, what is the best explanation for this improvement?
options: Employees respond better to financial incentives
The team felt more included and valued in decision-making
Stricter deadlines increased productivity
Independent work led to greater individual autonomy
hints: Notice the shift in Laura's style: moving from autocratic instruction to *participatory planning* and *integrating team ideas*.
Verify whether the theory treats leader style as fixed (requiring situational engineering) or adaptable to follower readiness and task ambiguity.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: b** — *The team felt more included and valued in decision-making.*
- **Why b works:** Participative leadership and procedural voice increase intrinsic buy-in, psychological ownership, and morale because members see their inputs valued in shared decisions.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `a` and `c` introduce financial rewards and strict deadlines, neither of which changed in the vignette.
  - `d` attributes the gain to solitary/independent work rather than *participatory planning* and *open dialogue*.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: and `c` introduce financial rewards and strict deadlines, neither of which changed in the vignette.

questions.title: Sample Exam · S14
questions.promptMarkdown: Sofia works as a junior analyst at a consulting firm. She has a stable salary, a permanent contract, and good relationships with her colleagues. Recently, however, she feels unchallenged and wants to take on more creative projects where she can grow her skills and contribute meaningfully. Based on Maslow's hierarchy of needs, which need is Sofia currently trying to fulfill?
options: Safety needs
Esteem needs
Physiological needs
Belongingness needs
Self-actualization needs
hints: Check which needs Sofia *already has satisfied* ("stable salary, permanent contract" = physiological/safety; "good relationships" = social/belongingness), then identify the top rung focused on creative skill growth and potential.
Check whether the driver comes from task enjoyment itself, fairness of rules/voice vs. outcomes, or multiplying effort-to-performance-to-reward beliefs.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: e** — *Self-actualization needs.*
- **Why e works:** Physiological & Safety needs (stable salary, permanent contract) and Social/Belongingness needs (good colleague relationships) are satisfied; Sofia's drive for creative challenge, skill growth, and realizing potential is **self-actualization**.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `a` (*Safety*), `c` (*Physiological*), and `d` (*Belongingness*) are explicitly satisfied already in the prompt.
  - `b` (*Esteem*) focuses on status, recognition, prestige, and external achievement rankings rather than intrinsic personal skill growth and creative self-fulfillment.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: (*Safety*), `c` (*Physiological*), and `d` (*Belongingness*) are explicitly satisfied already in the prompt.

questions.title: Sample Exam · S15
questions.promptMarkdown: An organization launches a cross-functional task force with 18 members to design a new onboarding program. During meetings, a few members contribute actively while several others put in minimal effort, assuming the rest of the group will cover for them. Which group dynamic is most likely occurring?
options: Group polarization
Social facilitation
Social loafing
Groupthink
Collective intelligence
hints: In large groups (here 18 members) where individual accountability blurs, people systematically expend less effort than when working alone.
Separate reduced effort in large groups (diffusion of responsibility) from suppressed dissent under unanimity pressure or genuine mutual-accountability synergy.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: c** — *Social loafing.*
- **Why c works:** **Social loafing** is the tendency for individuals to expend less effort when working collectively—especially in oversized teams—due to diffusion of responsibility ("assuming the rest of the group will cover for them").
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `a` (*Group polarization*) is attitude extremism after discussion.
  - `b` (*Social facilitation*) is *improved* performance on simple/well-learned tasks when watched.
  - `d` (*Groupthink*) is premature consensus suppressing dissent.
  - `e` (*Collective intelligence*) is a group's general ability across tasks, the opposite of free-riding.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: (*Group polarization*) is attitude extremism after discussion.

questions.promptMarkdown: At Nordway Electronics, junior technicians are unsure who to report to when technical glitches arise—some report to the production supervisor, while others contact the quality control manager. This lack of clarity violates which structural principle?
options: Span of control
Chain of command

questions.promptMarkdown: During a crucial meeting at a marketing firm, senior managers propose a bold new campaign strategy that involves high financial risk. questions.title: Tech & Structure · T1: Technology and gains in productivity
questions.promptMarkdown:
A bank gives its advisers an AI tool that writes loan reports. For two years, nothing improves, because the advisers keep writing the reports by hand as before. Then the bank changes the job: the AI writes the reports and the advisers only check them. Within a few months, each adviser handles twice as many loans.
Which explanation of the organization's choice best accounts for this?
options: Redistribution: one firm's gain is another firm's loss, so no new value is created
Lags: new technology takes many years to pay off, whatever the firm does
Organizational change and structure: gains come when the firm changes how tasks are divided, grouped and coordinated
Mismeasurement: the gains exist, but standard statistics fail to capture them
Technological determinism: the technology alone decides the outcome
hints: Recall Brynjolfsson, Rock & Syverson's J-curve / Solow Paradox explanations in Lesson 11: why did productivity double *only* after job roles changed from hand-writing to AI-drafting + adviser-checking?
Reject technological determinism: productivity and autonomy outcomes depend on how workflows, social norms, and opaque evaluation rules are enacted.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: C** — *Organizational change and structure: gains come when the firm changes how tasks are divided, grouped and coordinated.*
- **Why C works:** Merely installing AI yields the Solow Productivity Paradox ("investment without reorganization"). Only **complementary organizational restructuring**—changing division of labor, workflows, and coordination—unlocks the productivity surge.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` (*Redistribution*) argues total output never rises across firms, whereas here adviser output per person literally doubled inside the bank after workflow redesign.
  - `B` (*Lags*) claims waiting *passively* pays off "whatever the firm does", contradicting the fact that two years of waiting changed nothing until the *job design* changed.
  - `D` (*Mismeasurement*) blames statistics, whereas gains were zero until workflow changed.
  - `E` (*Technological determinism*) claims the software itself determines outcomes regardless of organizational choices—the exact thesis this vignette disproves.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: (*Redistribution*) argues total output never rises across firms, whereas here adviser output per person literally doubled inside the bank after workflow redesign.

According to Robbins & Judge, which structure best fits the innovation unit?

An organic structure with low formalization, decentralized decisions and cross-functional teams

A bureaucracy with a strict chain of command, to keep the uncertain work under control

questions.promptMarkdown:
A Norwegian hospital changes its procedure for how it treats hip-surgery patients. Before, each patient was passed between departments that worked one step at a time. Now every patient follows one standard fast-track plan from admission to discharge. The hospital buys no new equipment or software. A manager says: "This is not a technology change, because nothing new was installed."
According to Robbins & Judge's definition, is the manager right?

Yes: technology means digital tools such as software and AI
Yes: this is a change in culture, because staff work differently
No: technology is how an organization transfers its inputs into outputs
No, but only if the new plan raises productivity

questions.title: Slide Diagnostic D2 · Fiedler Contingency Check
questions.promptMarkdown: A manufacturing plant supervisor scores **low** on Fiedler's **LPC** questionnaire (`task-oriented`). She faces a **moderately favorable** situation: mediocre leader–member relations, structured assembly tasks, and moderate position power. Should senior management expect her to perform well, and if not, what does Fiedler recommend?

questions.title: Wiseflow Mock · Question 1
questions.promptMarkdown: A software division head notices that whenever an engineer misses a sprint deadline, colleagues attribute it to laziness, whereas when the division head misses a quarterly forecast, she immediately blames sudden macro interest-rate shocks. Which perceptual bias captures this *systematic asymmetry* between judging oneself versus judging others?
options: Selective perception
Actor–observer bias
Contrast effect
Stereotyping
Halo effect
hints: Pay close attention to the exact *two-sided contrast* in the prompt: explaining *others'* actions via internal traits vs. *one's own* actions via external circumstances.
Check whose behavior is being explained (only another person = FAE; comparing self vs. other = actor–observer; one trait coloring all ratings = halo).
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: B** — *Actor–observer bias.*
- **Why B works:** **Actor–observer bias** highlights the systematic asymmetry between how people explain *others'* outcomes (dispositional/internal traits) versus *their own* behavior (situational/external pressures). *(Note: Unlike `Sample S12`, which only examined Dr. Ahmed's observer judgment of Elena—classic FAE—this vignette explicitly contrasts both actor and observer viewpoints.)*
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` (*Selective perception*) = interpreting stimuli selectively based on one's background/interests.
  - `C` (*Contrast effect*) = judging a person better or worse by comparing them to someone encountered immediately prior.
  - `D` (*Stereotyping*) = judging someone based on group category assumptions.
  - `E` (*Halo effect*) = letting one positive/negative trait spill over to color every unrelated evaluation of the same person.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: (*Selective perception*) = interpreting stimuli selectively based on one's background/interests.

Assessment centers show high predictive validity for managerial potential, whereas forced ranking often discourages collaboration and generates internal competition
Both tools primarily measure cognitive intelligence and deliver identical predictive validity regardless of job level
Forced ranking eliminates leniency and halo errors without harming morale, while assessment centers only work for entry-level clerical roles
Written integrity tests outperform assessment centers on every managerial dimension and cost nothing to administer

questions.promptMarkdown: Freja loves her hospital's patient-centered mission and genuinely wants to stay at Oslo University Hospital (`high emotional attachment`), yet she secretly worries that after 15 years in a niche surgical specialty no private clinic would match her seniority benefits. According to Meyer & Allen's Three-Component Model, what distinguishes Freja from Lars?

Freja has strong affective commitment (alongside practical awareness of switching costs), whereas Lars exemplifies predominantly continuance commitment
Both exhibit identical continuance commitment because both consider financial costs
Lars demonstrates organizational citizenship behavior, whereas Freja demonstrates psychological withdrawal
Both exhibit high cognitive dissonance without any organizational commitment

questions.title: Wiseflow Mock · Question 6
questions.promptMarkdown: In an emergency trauma unit, errors carry lethal consequences, so the lead surgeon institutes strict clinical checklists alongside weekly "near-miss confessions" where residents openly analyze mistakes without ridicule or blame. Under Amy Edmondson's (1999) `Psychological Safety × Accountability` matrix, where does this team operate, and what outcome should OB predict?
options: Comfort Zone — high camaraderie and low error reporting
Anxiety Zone — high performance targets paired with fear of speaking up
Apathy Zone — low standards and passive disengagement
Learning / High-Performance Zone — open error learning paired with rigorous quality execution
Groupthink Zone — high conformity eliminating task conflict
hints: Plot both axes carefully: **Strict checklists / lethal standards** = High Accountability; **Near-miss confessions without ridicule** = High Psychological Safety.
Separate reduced effort in large groups (diffusion of responsibility) from suppressed dissent under unanimity pressure or genuine mutual-accountability synergy.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: D** — *Learning / High-Performance Zone — open error learning paired with rigorous quality execution.*
- **Why D works:** Edmondson explicitly warns that Psychological Safety is **not** lowering standards ("being nice"). High Psychological Safety + High Accountability creates the **Learning Zone**, enabling candid mistake detection and continuous improvement.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` (*Comfort Zone*) = High Safety + **Low** Accountability (missing here due to strict checklists).
  - `B` (*Anxiety Zone*) = **Low** Safety + High Accountability (missing here because mistakes are welcomed openly without blame).
  - `C` (*Apathy Zone*) = Low Safety + Low Accountability.

questions.title: Wiseflow Mock · Question 7
questions.promptMarkdown: Frederick Luthans observed over 450 real-world managers to test whether what makes managers get **promoted fast** equals what makes their teams **perform effectively**. What was his central empirical finding?
options: Managers who spent the most time on Human Resource Management were promoted fastest
Networking had the strongest link to *rapid promotion* (managerial "success"), whereas Communication and HR Management drove *effective team performance*
Traditional management (planning and controlling) was equally useless for both promotion and unit performance
Effective managers spent 70% of their time socializing outside the firm
Communication predicted rapid promotion twice as strongly as networking did
hints: Remember the sharp irony of **Luthans' "Successful vs. Effective Managers"**: *Success* = speed of promotion; *Effectiveness* = unit quantity/quality + team satisfaction. Which activity dominated which outcome?
Eliminate choices using absolute words like 'only' or 'always'—OB relies on contingency variables and distinguishing planning (defining goals) from organizing/executing.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: B** — *Networking had the strongest link to rapid promotion (managerial "success"), whereas Communication and HR Management drove effective team performance.*
- **Why B works:** Luthans found **Successful managers** (promoted fastest) devoted `48%` of their time to **networking** and only `11%` to HRM, whereas **Effective managers** (high unit output & satisfied teams) spent `44%` on **communication** and `26%` on **HRM** (`11%` networking).
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` and `E` reverse the percentages for networking vs. HRM/communication.
  - `C` exaggerates; traditional management still formed ~19–32% of work.
  - `D` misstates the percentage (`48%`, not `70%`, for successful managers' networking).
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: and `E` reverse the percentages for networking vs. HRM/communication.

questions.title: Wiseflow Mock · Question 8
questions.promptMarkdown: A hotel concierge smiles warmly and greets demanding guests enthusiastically even while grieving a personal family loss. Inside, she works hard to genuinely *remember happy family memories* so that her warmth actually feels sincere rather than plastered on. How would *Hochschild / Robbins & Judge (Ch. 4)* classify her internal emotion-regulation strategy?
options: Surface acting — faking outward smiles without changing inner feelings, raising burnout
Deep acting — actively modifying inner feelings to align with organizational display rules
Emotional dissonance maximization — amplifying felt misery to signal authenticity
Affective events disruption — passive mood contagion from angry guests
Compassion fatigue — complete loss of felt empathy
hints: Compare changing only the **facial mask** (`Surface acting`) vs. deliberately cultivating the **underlying felt emotion** (`Deep acting`).
Separate faking outward expressions (surface acting) from modifying inner feelings (deep acting), and check job demands against job control/resources.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: B** — *Deep acting — actively modifying inner feelings to align with organizational display rules.*
- **Why B works:** Working internally to evoke genuine feelings matching the required display rule defines **deep acting**, which causes less emotional exhaustion than hollow **surface acting**.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` (*Surface acting*) fakes outward expressions without altering inner feelings (higher dissonance and burnout).
  - `C` and `E` misread her deliberate positive reappraisal.

questions.pitfall: Distractor check: (*Surface acting*) fakes outward expressions without altering inner feelings (higher dissonance and burnout).

questions.title: Wiseflow Mock · Question 9
questions.promptMarkdown: Under *Conservation of Resources (COR) Theory* (`Hobfoll`, *R&J Ch. 18*) and the *Job Demands–Resources (JD-R)* model, why does chronic workload without autonomy or recovery time accelerate into full clinical **burnout**?
options: Challenge stressors automatically convert into hindrance stressors after 90 days
Resource depletion triggers defensive "loss spirals" because employees lack buffers (`autonomy, support`) to replenish energy against overwhelming job demands
Effort–Reward Imbalance occurs only when base salary falls below national minimum wage
High emotional stability causes employees to ignore workplace stressors until sudden collapse
Hindrance stressors increase engagement whenever managerial demands remain ambiguous
hints: Separate **JD-R** (`Demands` deplete vs. `Resources` buffer/motivate) and **COR** (*resource loss weighs heavier than equivalent gain* -> defensive `loss spirals`).
Separate faking outward expressions (surface acting) from modifying inner feelings (deep acting), and check job demands against job control/resources.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: B** — *Resource depletion triggers defensive "loss spirals" because employees lack buffers (autonomy, support) to replenish energy against overwhelming job demands.*
- **Why B works:** Both **COR Theory** (loss of energy/time resources sparks accelerating **loss spirals** when recovery/buffers fail) and **JD-R** (unbuffered high demands exhaust energy → emotional exhaustion, cynicism, reduced efficacy) explain burnout via structural demand–resource imbalance.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` invents an arbitrary `90-day` threshold.
  - `C` reduces **Effort–Reward Imbalance (ERI)** to minimum-wage law rather than subjective effort vs. pay/esteem/career security imbalance.
  - `D` is false: emotional stability buffers stress rather than causing sudden collapse.
  - `E` inverts the hindrance–challenge distinction: *hindrance* stressors (role ambiguity, red tape) consistently *reduce* engagement.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: invents an arbitrary `90-day` threshold.

questions.title: Wiseflow Mock · Question 10
questions.promptMarkdown: Chris Argyris contrasts **single-loop learning** with **double-loop learning** (`Lesson 13`). Which example illustrates **double-loop learning** in a retail bank?

When digital customer complaints rise, executives adjust call-center response time targets from 45 seconds to 30 seconds

Staff memorize updated compliance PDFs before an annual audit

questions.title: Wiseflow Mock · Question 11
questions.promptMarkdown: A cross-departmental product team consists of engineers and marketing managers who share passionate, heated arguments over **what architecture best serves future users** (`which features to prioritize`), yet trust one another personally and enjoy grabbing coffee after meetings. Which type of conflict are they experiencing, and what does OB research predict?
options: Relationship conflict — always destroys team performance regardless of intensity
Process conflict — consistently boosts strategic creativity when unaddressed
Task conflict at moderate levels — can stimulate discussion, scrutiny of assumptions, and creative decision quality when psychological safety is high
Role conflict — requires immediate downsizing to restore unity of command
Distributive conflict — forces zero-sum win-lose outcomes
hints: Separate the three conflict types (`Task`, `Relationship`, `Process`) and recall De Dreu & Weingart / `R&J` findings: only *one* type at *moderate* levels under *high trust* can improve creativity.
Separate formal position power (legitimate/reward/coercive) from personal power (expert/referent), and weigh resource nonsubstitutability plus each side's walk-away alternative.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: C** — *Task conflict at moderate levels — can stimulate discussion, scrutiny of assumptions, and creative decision quality when psychological safety is high.*
- **Why C works:** Disagreement over work *content and goals* ("which features/architecture") paired with strong interpersonal warmth ("grabbing coffee") is **task conflict** (without toxic relationship conflict), which in moderate doses raises critical inquiry and creative problem solving when trust/psych safety is present.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` (*Relationship conflict*) involves personal animosity/friction—explicitly absent here.
  - `B` (*Process conflict*) concerns *how* work gets delegated/sequenced, and high process conflict usually harms performance by breeding role uncertainty.
  - `D` and `E` misdiagnose healthy goal-oriented debate as formal role overload or zero-sum bargaining.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: (*Relationship conflict*) involves personal animosity/friction—explicitly absent here.

questions.promptMarkdown: According to *Edmondson* and *Gersick's Punctuated Equilibrium Model*, when does a temporary project group (`e.g., 8-week student consulting project`) typically experience its abrupt burst of urgency, drop old assumptions, and adopt major new work perspectives?
options: Immediately during the Forming stage in Week 1
Precisely at the **midpoint** between its first meeting and its official deadline (`Week 4`), after initial inertia
Only after final deliverables are graded
Gradually and smoothly at a constant weekly slope from Week 1 to Week 8
Whenever the group eliminates all task deadlines
hints: Contrast **Tuckman's** sequential 5 stages (`Forming–Storming–Norming–Performing–Adjourning`) with **Gersick's Punctuated Equilibrium**: temporary deadline-bound groups freeze their Phase 1 direction until a dramatic alarm clock rings halfway!

questions.title: Wiseflow Mock · Question 14
questions.promptMarkdown: Two senior directors at a Danish wind-energy firm disagree over how to split an R&D budget. Director A wants 100% allocated to offshore turbines; Director B wants 100% in grid batteries. Instead of steamrolling each other or lazily splitting 50/50 without thinking, they map underlying needs (`A needs offshore reliability telemetry; B needs storage smoothing`) and craft a joint `hybrid offshore-battery demonstrator` that captures external EU grant funding, expanding total resources for both units. Which Thomas–Kilmann style is this?
options: Avoiding
Accommodating
Compromising
Collaborating
Competing
hints: Plot **Assertiveness** (`high/low`) × **Cooperativeness** (`high/low`). Distinguish giving up half (`Compromising`: midpoint split) from **integrating both interests to expand the pie** (`Collaborating`).
Separate formal position power (legitimate/reward/coercive) from personal power (expert/referent), and weigh resource nonsubstitutability plus each side's walk-away alternative.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: D** — *Collaborating.*
- **Why D works:** **Collaborating** (`high assertiveness + high cooperativeness`) probes underlying interests and invents an integrative win-win solution (`EU-funded hybrid demonstrator`) that fully satisfies both parties' core goals rather than cutting each in half.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` (*Avoiding*) = low assertiveness, low cooperativeness.
  - `B` (*Accommodating*) = low assertiveness, high cooperativeness (yielding one's own needs).
  - `C` (*Compromising*) = moderate both; each side gives something up in a pure split without expanding value—explicitly ruled out in the stem ("rather than lazily splitting 50/50").
  - `E` (*Competing*) = high assertiveness, low cooperativeness.

questions.title: Wiseflow Mock · Question 15
questions.promptMarkdown: In *Leader–Member Exchange (LMX) Theory*, managers almost always form high-trust, privileged **"in-group"** ties with select subordinates while maintaining formal, contractual **"out-group"** ties with others. Research (`R&J Ch. 12`) confirms that in-group members perform higher and quit less often. What subtle *dark side* must leaders watch out for when managing LMX?

Out-group members often experience perceived procedural/interpersonal unfairness, lower morale, and cynicism if in-group access seems closed or biased
LMX requires identical treatment of all followers, eliminating dyadic differences
Out-group members exhibit excessive organizational citizenship behavior
LMX focuses solely on charismatic speeches rather than two-way relationships
hints: Contrast LMX's core strength (high-quality dyadic trust boosts in-group output) against equity/justice risks for those excluded from the inner circle.

questions.title: Wiseflow Mock · Question 23
questions.promptMarkdown: Which combination of **Kelley's Attribution Cues** would lead an observer (`e.g., manager Ingrid`) to conclude that employee Jonas's stellar quarterly presentation was caused by **internal ability/effort** rather than an **external stroke of luck**?
options: High distinctiveness, high consensus, low consistency
Low distinctiveness, low consensus, high consistency
High distinctiveness, low consensus, low consistency
Low distinctiveness, high consensus, low consistency
High distinctiveness, high consensus, high consistency
hints:
Test each cue logically on a **positive** outcome:
- **Low Distinctiveness**: Does Jonas deliver great work across *many* different projects, not just this easy one? Yes → **Internal**!
- **Low Consensus**: Did *other* colleagues fail or do much worse on this same task? Yes → **Internal**!
- **High Consistency**: Does Jonas do this reliably *over time*? Yes → **Internal**!

questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: B** — *Low distinctiveness, low consensus, high consistency.*
- **Why B works:** In Kelley's covariation model, an **internal attribution** emerges when the person acts this way across *different situations* (**low distinctiveness**), behaves differently from peers in the same situation (**low consensus**), and does so reliably over time (**high consistency**).

  - `A` (`High D, High C, Low Cons`) points to a situational anomaly.

questions.promptMarkdown: Two deeply dissatisfied hospital pharmacists react differently to unsafe staffing cuts. Using *Farrell's EVLN Framework* (`Exit–Voice–Loyalty–Neglect`, *R&J Ch. 3*), how are Ingrid and Thomas classified?

Ingrid = Exit; Thomas = Loyalty

questions.title: Wiseflow Mock · Question 30
questions.promptMarkdown: An engineering team already has **specific, measurable sprint deadlines** (`Goal-Setting Theory`), yet performance stays flat because the targets were set so outrageously high (`300% impossible speedups`) with zero manager confidence-building that workers simply give up inside. Under *Locke & Latham* and *Bandura's Self-Efficacy*, what critical mechanism broke down?
options: Specific goals always reduce effort regardless of difficulty
Goals motivate best when they are **challenging yet attainable AND employees feel high self-efficacy / goal commitment**—not impossible targets that shatter confidence
Vague "do your best" goals outperform specific quantitative goals under high stress
Goal-Setting Theory applies only to hourly assembly lines, never to engineering
Feedback weakens Goal-Setting motivation by creating anxiety
hints: Remember the boundary conditions on Locke & Latham's **Goal-Setting Theory**: Difficulty boosts performance *only* up to the point where the person accepts/commits to the goal and believes it's achievable (**Self-Efficacy**)! Also notice **Galatea/Pygmalion** confidence boosters.
Check whether the driver comes from task enjoyment itself, fairness of rules/voice vs. outcomes, or multiplying effort-to-performance-to-reward beliefs.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: B** — *Goals motivate best when they are challenging yet attainable AND employees feel high self-efficacy / goal commitment—not impossible targets that shatter confidence.*
- **Why B works:** Specific, challenging goals lift output only when paired with **goal commitment**, **task feedback**, and adequate **self-efficacy** (`belief that you can succeed`). Impossible goals crush self-efficacy and break commitment.

questions.title: Wiseflow Mock · Question 31
questions.promptMarkdown: A call-center supervisor wants her agents to submit error-free daily compliance logs by 16:00. She announces: *"Everyone who completes an error-free compliance log by 16:00 gets exempted from Friday afternoon's tedious data-cleanup shift."* Which operant conditioning / **Reinforcement Theory** mechanism is the supervisor using?
options: Punishment — adding an unpleasant consequence to suppress an unwanted behavior
Extinction — withholding all positive consequences until a behavior disappears
Negative reinforcement — **removing an unpleasant condition** (`tedious Friday shift`) to **increase** a desired behavior (`timely error-free logs`)
Positive reinforcement — adding a financial cash bonus
Cognitive dissonance — changing attitudes after contradictory actions
hints: Classic Wiseflow trap! **Reinforcement** ALWAYS aims to **INCREASE** desired behavior; **Punishment** aims to **DECREASE** unwanted behavior. *Positive* = add something pleasant; *Negative* = remove something unpleasant!
Check whether the driver comes from task enjoyment itself, fairness of rules/voice vs. outcomes, or multiplying effort-to-performance-to-reward beliefs.
questions.solutionMarkdown:
**Correct Answer: C** — *Negative reinforcement — removing an unpleasant condition (tedious Friday shift) to increase a desired behavior (timely error-free logs).*
- **Why C works:** **Negative reinforcement** strengthens desired behavior by *terminating or withdrawing an aversive/unpleasant stimulus* contingent on doing the right thing.
- **Why distractors fail:**
  - `A` (*Punishment*) suppresses *unwanted* behavior by inflicting something negative or removing something pleasant—here the target is *increasing* accurate log submission!
  - `B` (*Extinction*) eliminates previously rewarded behavior by ignoring/withdrawing positive reinforcement.
  - `D` (*Positive reinforcement*) adds a pleasant stimulus (praise, bonus) rather than removing an unpleasant shift.
  - `E` belongs to attitude theory (`Festinger`), not operant conditioning.
questions.pitfall: Distractor check: (*Punishment*) suppresses *unwanted* behavior by inflicting something negative or removing something pleasant—here the target is *increasing* accurate log submission!

questions.title: Wiseflow Mock · Question 32
questions.promptMarkdown: A community open-source developer has spent Saturdays happily building free accessibility plugins out of pure passion (`high intrinsic motivation`). When a corporate sponsor steps in offering **controlling micro-bounties (`\$15 per tiny bug closed with mandatory hourly tracking screenshots`)**, the developer's enthusiasm dries up completely and she stops contributing as soon as the bounties pause. Which theory explains why adding external pay *backfired*?

Cognitive Evaluation Theory / Self-Determination Theory — controlling external rewards shifted perceived causality outward, eroding autonomy and crowding out intrinsic motivation

Equity Theory — because her colleagues earned `\$16`
Scientific Management — Taylor proved small micro-bonuses always improve creative joy

questions.title: Wiseflow Mock · Question 33
questions.promptMarkdown: Before negotiating a vendor contract, a procurement lead reads an industry blog mentioning an absurdly high `\$1,200/seat` enterprise license price. Even though she knows that figure came from an unrelated luxury software vendor, her subsequent mental adjustments drift upward and she happily signs a `\$950/seat` contract when historical benchmarks justified `\$650/seat`. Meanwhile, her CFO delays buying a safe airline route simply because a dramatic crash dominated television news all week. Which pair of biases misled the procurement lead and the CFO respectively?
options: Confirmation bias (lead) and Escalation of commitment (CFO)
Anchoring bias (lead) and Availability bias (CFO)
Hindsight bias (lead) and Randomness error (CFO)
Representativeness heuristic (lead) and Overconfidence bias (CFO)
System 2 over-analysis (lead) and Bounded rationality (CFO)

Match both cues:
1. Fixating on an initial arbitrary number (`\$1,200`) and failing to adjust enough down → **Anchoring**.
2. Overestimating rare plane crash likelihood because vivid news coverage makes it mentally easy to recall → **Availability**.

**Correct Answer: B** — *Anchoring bias (lead) and Availability bias (CFO).*

Collaborating to competing
